ns2:section.sectionText: SP25 - ENGL 350 - Writing About Literature, Text, and Culture - Rats, Literature, and Science - Lucinda Cole - Both in literature and science, rodents—especially rats and mice—have long been treated as “mirror animals.” Fables, poems, and horror stories use them to dramatize the most feared features of humanity, such as greed, lust, or physical corruption. In biomedical research, they are the preferred animals for pre-clinical trails, in part because they share with us 95% of approximately 30,000 genes. This course examines how relationships between and among humans and rats have been shaped by literature and science, by epidemics and experiments. Works will include Robert Browning, “The Pied Piper of Hamelin”; Edgar Alan Poe, “The Pit and the Pendulum”; Bram Stoker, “The Judge’s House” and “The Burial of the Rats”; Sigmund Freud, “The Rat Man”; Ernst Weiss, “The Rat Ship”; Stephen Gilbert, Ratman’s Notebooks; Robert C. O’Brien, Mrs. Frisby and the Rats of NIMH; and James Herbert The Rats (1974), read alongside contemporary scientific studies of, for example, cholera, bubonic plague, population density, and “creative deviancy.” We will end with a section on rats and indigenous knowledges.
